reference.source: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology / Rook's Textbook of Dermatology
clinicalPearls: Miliaria arises from blockage of eccrine sweat ducts, so it favours hot, humid conditions, febrile illness, occlusion, and overdressing, and is common in neonates and in the newly bedridden

The subtype reflects the depth of duct obstruction: crystallina shows tiny clear, easily ruptured superficial vesicles; rubra produces itchy or prickly erythematous papulovesicles; and the deeper profunda presents as firm, skin-coloured papules
Typical sites are areas of occlusion and friction such as the trunk, flexures, and skin under clothing or dressings
In infants it commonly affects the neck, groin, and axillae and is easily provoked by warm environments and heavy wrapping
The cornerstone of management is cooling and reducing sweating: a cooler environment, loose breathable clothing, and avoiding occlusion, which allow the ducts to reopen
It is generally self-limiting once the provoking heat and occlusion are removed, and specific drug treatment is rarely needed
Widespread deep miliaria can impair sweating and predispose to heat intolerance and, in extreme heat, heat exhaustion
Secondary bacterial infection (miliaria pustulosa) can complicate the picture if lesions are scratched or persist
reference.pathophysiology: Miliaria results from obstruction of the eccrine sweat ducts, which causes sweat to leak into the surrounding skin rather than reach the surface. Keratin plugging of the duct, often aggravated by an overgrowth of skin flora producing occlusive material, blocks flow at varying levels. The level of the block determines the clinical form: obstruction within the stratum corneum causes the superficial vesicles of crystallina, blockage within the epidermis produces the inflammatory papulovesicles of rubra, and obstruction at the dermo-epidermal junction gives the deeper papules of profunda. The extravasated sweat provokes local inflammation and the sensation of prickling, while widespread duct blockage can compromise thermoregulation.
additionalDifferentials: Neonatal erythema toxicum or transient neonatal pustular melanosis
Grover's disease (transient acantholytic dermatosis) in adults
additionalInvestigations: Diagnosis is clinical, based on morphology and a history of heat, occlusion, or fever
Skin swab if secondary bacterial infection (pustular miliaria) is suspected
Investigations are seldom required, and biopsy is reserved for atypical or persistent cases
Assessment of the environment and clothing or dressing practices, especially in infants and bedridden patients
redFlags: Extensive deep (profunda) involvement impairing sweating with symptoms of heat intolerance or heat exhaustion
Signs of secondary bacterial infection such as pustules, increasing pain, or spreading erythema
Systemic upset or fever suggesting an alternative or complicating diagnosis
Failure to settle after removing heat and occlusion, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Miliaria is benign and typically resolves quickly once overheating and occlusion are addressed; recurrence is common with repeated heat exposure, and only extensive deep disease or secondary infection causes significant problems.
pitfalls: Treating with occlusive creams or heavy dressings that worsen duct blockage
Overwrapping or overdressing infants and perpetuating the rash
Mistaking pustular miliaria with secondary infection for a primary bacterial folliculitis or vice versa
Overlooking impaired thermoregulation in extensive deep disease during hot conditions
management: Cool the patient and reduce sweating with a cooler, less humid environment and air conditioning to allow the ducts to reopen
Wear loose, breathable clothing and avoid occlusive fabrics, dressings and overdressing
In infants, avoid heavy wrapping and keep the neck, groin and axillae cool and dry
Relieve the itch and prickling of miliaria rubra with cooling measures and, if needed, a short course of a topical corticosteroid
Treat secondary bacterial infection (pustular miliaria) with topical or systemic antibiotics guided by swab
Reassure that the condition is self-limiting once overheating and occlusion are removed, and advise avoiding future heat exposure to prevent recurrence
